content:
Yesterday Levent Alpöge announced an (unformalized) construction of a complex structure on S6S^6S6, resolving a long-standing conjecture due to Hopf. It is currently in the process of being formalized by Dean Cureton and @Paul Lezeau.

Today, I opened a PR to Lean Eval (cc @Kim Morrison) adding a simple challenge file:

instance instChartedSpaceS6 :
    ChartedSpace (EuclideanSpace ℂ (Fin 3))
      (Metric.sphere (0 : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 7)) 1) :=
  sorry

instance instIsManifoldS6 :
    IsManifold 𝓘(ℂ, EuclideanSpace ℂ (Fin 3)) ω
      (Metric.sphere (0 : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 7)) 1) :=
  sorry

This challenge unfortunately does not give any information about how the complex structure is actually constructed: In particular, whether it uses Alpöge's family of complex 2-tori whose periods are the modular functions of the (3,4,∞) triangle group. This is relevant because Alpöge's construction directly contradicts a paper of Campana-Demailly-Peternell.

Another claimed proof of this result by Gabor Etesi, published in the Journal of Mathematical Physics in 2015 received much less attention, and does not contradict Campana-Demailly-Peternell. Etesi's paper was subsequently disputed by Robert Bryant on Mathoverflow, but Etesi claimed to fix the issue in an erratum. (AI claims there's also another issue with this erratum; I can not find any discussion of it online)

Assuming the formalization effort is successful, the above spec gives us a resolution of the S6S^6S6 question, but still does not give a clear answer as to:

  • Which, if either, of the two constructions above are correct
  • The status of Campana-Demailly-Peternell's paper
  • Who should be credited with the resolution of this conjecture

Does anyone have any ideas on how to distinguish between these possible constructions in Lean? (without significantly increasing the surface area for humans to review)

Have you tried to ask AI for such a distinguishing criteria? Maybe there is a property that one construction claims to have that the other doesn’t (perhaps around this CDP-paper).

This could also be a good MathOverflow question if asked right.

Or if not, once it is formalized, one could have AI inspect the formalization for which paper it followed (and maybe again ask for how different the proof would look using the other method).
Isn't the burden of proof with Levent to show why his claims hold water? Especially if they contradict the CDP paper?

From what I saw, the errors in CDP20 have been known since 2 years ago (quote: "the issue with the validity of CDP for algebraic dim 1 was already noticed by Honda-Viaclovsky https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.05035v2 (see the difference between v1 and v2...).") and become widely recognized in the community after yesterday's announcement. Interestingly, CDP20 is itself a correction of CDP98, which was found to be problematic by Lehn, Rollenske, and Schinko in https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.09719.

Yes I agree, I am nearly certain that CDP20 is wrong and Alpöge is correct. However, is there a way to express this with a Lean spec without already being a subject-matter expert on these papers? I raise this example to ponder the gap in Lean's refereeing power in a social context with multiple competing papers.

Showing that the fibration S⁶ → S² is a holomorphic map (ℂ-ContMDiff) should be sufficient to contradict CDP (alg dim 0 means no nonconstant meromorphic function) and rule out Etesi's claimed construction. You might want to copy the definition of the Riemann sphere here, or otherwise state that there exists two nonconstant holomorphic functions f, g from open sets U, V in S⁶ to ℂ such that U and V cover S⁶ and fg=1 on U ∩ V.

Here's an AI-digested 21-page version of the complex S^6 construction, courtesy of Prof. Mingchen Xia, in case it's useful: A Proposed Construction of a Complex Structure on S6
It's probably better for human consumption (everyone thinks the 108-page writeup is far too long) but I have no idea if it's easier / has all the details for formalization.

Minor comment: neither your formalization of the statement nor Formal Conjectures' version requires that the smooth structure on S⁶ agrees with the standard one, but it seems this is usually understood as a part of the problem, and the Claude writeup quoted nonexistence of exotic 6-spheres to address this; I don't think this needs to be part of the formalization though.

But the topological 6D Poincare conjecture is still needed for the proof: it's fair to assume it, but it might be possible to circumvent it by working out more details: https://x.com/i/status/2091884731927547992

By the way, someone on Zhihu raised the interesting question about identifying the homotopy class of the fibration S⁶ → S² as an element in π₆(S²) ≅ ℤ⧸12ℤ: is it of order 1,2,3,4,6, or 12 (a generator, like the Hopf fibration)?

I guess we've all seen
#AI authored projects > Complex structure on S^6
and I wonder if this helps the above discussion.

I think they might have proven some statement like

ContMDiff (modelWithCornersSelf ℂ (ℂ × ComplexPlane₂)) (modelWithCornersSelf ℂ ℂ) ω SpecialPeriods.Threefold.projectionSphere

but it was cut out of the released file since it's not in the transitive closure of the final challenge statement.
